guide.markdown:
Express.js (expressjs/express) — Onboarding Guide

Summary

* What it is: Fast, unopinionated, minimalist web framework for Node.js
* Repo: https://github.com/expressjs/express
* Docs: https://expressjs.com
* Minimum Node.js: 18+

1. Project overview
Express provides:

* A minimal core focused on HTTP servers and middleware composition
* Routing, request/response helpers, view rendering hooks, and content negotiation
* High test coverage and a rich ecosystem of official and community middleware

At a glance, the core code lives in lib/ and exposes:

* application.js — App instance methods (e.g., app.use, app.get, app.listen)
* request.js — Adds Express-specific helpers to Node’s IncomingMessage
* response.js — Adds helpers to ServerResponse (e.g., res.json, res.send, res.status)
* utils.js — Utilities used internally
* view.js — The View abstraction used for template rendering
* express.js — The main factory that produces an app instance

Examples demonstrating key features are under examples/, and the comprehensive test suite is under test/ using Mocha and Supertest.

2. Prerequisites

* Node.js 18 or newer
* npm (bundled with Node.js)

Optional (helpful for contributors):

* Git
* A REST client (curl, HTTPie, Postman) for manual testing
* Redis (only for specific examples that mention it)
* A code editor with ESLint support

3. Setup
Clone and install:

```
git clone https://github.com/expressjs/express.git
```
`cd express`
`npm install`
Useful scripts:

* Lint: npm run lint
* Tests: npm test
* Coverage (HTML + text): npm run test-cov
* CI-style coverage (lcov + text): npm run test-ci
* TAP reporter: npm run test-tap

4. Running it locally
Express is a library, not a standalone server. You generally:

* Run examples provided in the repo, or
* Create a tiny local app that imports the library from the repo root.

Option A — Run an example

```
# from repo root after npm install
```
`node examples/hello-world`
`# or any other example, for instance:`
`node examples/content-negotiation`
Then visit http://localhost:3000 (or the port the example prints).
Option B — Create a scratch app that uses your local checkout
Create scratch.js in the repo root:

```
// scratch.js (CommonJS)
```
`const express = require('.');`
`const app = express();`
`app.get('/', (req, res) => {`
`  res.send('Hello from local Express checkout!');`
`});`
`app.listen(3000, () => {`
`  console.log('Server running at http://localhost:3000');`
`});`
Run it:

```
node scratch.js
```

Option C — Use your local checkout in another project (optional)

* Create or open a separate app (with its own package.json)
* Link your local Express:

```
# in Express repo
```
`npm link`
`# in your separate app`
`npm link express`
Now require('express') in that app points to your local checkout.
Note on express-generator (optional)
For quickly scaffolding a full example app:

```
npm install -g express-generator@4
```
`express myapp`
`cd myapp`
`npm install`
`npm start`
This is separate from working on the core library, but it’s a handy way to see Express in action.

5. Project structure
Top-level

* Readme.md — Project intro, features, quick start
* History.md — Changelog
* LICENSE — MIT license
* package.json — Metadata, scripts, dependencies, Node engine (>= 18)
* index.js — Package entry that re-exports the core from lib/
* .editorconfig, .eslintrc.yml, .eslintignore, .gitignore, .npmrc — Tooling/config files
* .github/ — Issue templates, workflows, and repo metadata

Source (core)

* lib/
   * application.js — App methods and lifecycle
   * express.js — App factory
   * request.js — Request helpers
   * response.js — Response helpers
   * utils.js — Internal utilities
   * view.js — Template/view support

Examples (runnable)

* examples/
   * hello-world — Minimal server
   * content-negotiation — Negotiating response formats
   * cookies, cookie-sessions, session — Cookie and session basics
   * ejs, markdown — Template engine usage
   * error, error-pages — Error handling patterns
   * multi-router, route-*, route-separation — Router organization
   * mvc — Simple MVC-ish structure
   * static-files — Serving static assets
   * vhost — Virtual hosts
   * and more (see examples/README.md)

Tests and test support

* test/
   * acceptance/ — Higher-level behavior tests
   * fixtures/ — Static files and data for tests
   * support/ — Test bootstrap (e.g., environment)
   * Numerous unit/behavior tests covering app, req, res, routing, and utilities

6. Testing
Install dependencies once:

```
npm install
```

Run the full suite:

```
npm test
```

Common testing workflows:

* Run a single file:

```
npx mocha --require test/support/env --reporter spec --check-leaks test/res.json.js
```

* Filter tests by name:

```
npm test -- -g "res.json"
```
`# or with mocha directly`
`npx mocha --require test/support/env --reporter spec --check-leaks test/ -g "res.json"`

* Generate coverage:

```
npm run test-cov
```
`# Opens coverage in coverage/index.html (HTML report)`

* Lint before pushing:

```
npm run lint
```
`# or auto-fix where possible`
`npm run lint:fix`

Notes and tips

* Node version: Ensure Node.js 18+ to match engines in package.json and the README.
* Examples: Some examples mention additional packages (e.g., redis). Follow the example’s README or inline comments to install extras.
* Debug logging: Many dependencies use debug. You can enable namespaced logs, for example:

```
DEBUG=express:* npm test
```
`DEBUG=express:* node examples/hello-world`

Resources

* Repo README: https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/master/Readme.md
* Contributing guide: https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/master/Contributing.md
* Website & docs: https://expressjs.com
* Security policy: https://github.com/expressjs/express/security/policy

Advanced details (optional)
- Core runtime dependencies (from package.json) include body-parser, finalhandler, send, serve-static, router, http-errors, and more. Express composes these focused utilities instead of re-implementing them. - Tests rely on mocha, supertest, and nyc for coverage.Some examples demonstrate sessions, auth, or Redis-backed features. If an example errors with “module not found,” install the needed package in the repo root, e.g.: ```bash npm install redis connect-redis node examples/online ``` Always check the example’s comments for exact extras.If you prefer ESM syntax: 1) Create scratch.mjs in the repo root: ```js import express from '.';
const app = express();
app.get('/', (req, res) => res.send('Hello ESM!'));
app.listen(3000, () => console.log('http://localhost:3000'));
```
2) Run with:
```bash
node scratch.mjs
```
